generation.hypothesis: Enhanced sampling methods, such as metadynamics or umbrella sampling combined with thermodynamic integration, can accurately and efficiently compute melting properties (melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting) and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys.

generation.intervention: Application of advanced sampling techniques tailored to overcome high free-energy barriers: specifically, metadynamics or umbrella sampling combined with thermodynamic integration to traverse the solid–liquid transition.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed under high-temperature equilibrium near the melting point with controlled pressure and temperature to mimic experimental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Free energy landscape features governing the phase transition, including the transformation of local atomic order and diffusion across the phase boundary, which determine thermodynamic properties.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling navigates the complex energy landscape characteristic of high-entropy alloys, ensuring adequate sampling of rare events and improved convergence of free energy differences between the solid and liquid phases, thereby allowing accurate estimation of melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume changes at melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: The advanced sampling methods will yield melting properties and liquid-phase thermodynamic characteristics with improved accuracy (potentially reducing relative errors by roughly 10-20% compared to conventional techniques) and efficiency over traditional DSC measurements or standard molecular dynamics approaches.

generation.boundary: This approach is applicable across a range of high-entropy alloys near their melting temperature under equilibrium conditions, with its performance potentially varying with alloy composition and degree of configurational complexity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of error reduction and efficiency gains remains uncertain and may depend on specific alloy compositions and system sizes; quantitative performance improvements are estimated but require experimental validation.
